HONG KONG, China (CNN) -- From the runway to the store rack, Vivienne Tam is one designer who uses creativity and business acumen in equal measure. Leading fashion designer Vivienne Tam spoke to CNN's Andrew Stevens in The Boardroom. Since her start in the fashion business in the early '80s and establishing her own brand in the '90s, she has risen to fame with her east-meets-west styles. Today it's her skills in business which have expanded the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to talk about what it's like to lead both the business and creative direction of a global fashion line. Tam: The business side is like designing, it's like I like the touch of the fabric, I like to know the details about it. And you feel about it, you know about the deal, because who's the person who knows what the best deal for you is? Yourself. It's like designing clothes, I love to know how to solve every single thing, you know. Like what kind of budget . Stevens: It's just natural curiosity? Tam: Natural curiosity, I love it. I love every aspect of it. Stevens: Who have you learned your business skills from or have you made it up as you went along? Tam: I self-taught myself in business; I know nothing about the business, I learned everything -- about the pricing, the shipping, the contracts, everything -- by doing it. When you're doing it yourself, you know everything. If you don't do it, you just listen to somebody telling you how to do it, you're not experiencing it. Once you're experiencing it, you can grow so much from it. Once you experience it, you can go further, much further. It's a feeling of it. Stevens: When you won the Hong Kong businesswoman of the year award, you said that your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you? Tam: She inspired me so much you know, like you say, the determination, persistence. When she really wanted to make something, she would really go to the end, she'd really want to make it happen and I see her, she's really the force behind me. We were quite poor, we had no money, my parents were working really hard. When I grew up, I saw them working so hard, and then deep inside myself that I wanted to change the situation, I wanted to make something, this one thing. Stevens: What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson? Tam: For me, it's most important, a vision, determination, and to never say no to yourself. And be open to criticisms, open to learning, and open to criticisms and knowing nothing about the business; nothing, so you can learn everything by knowing nothing, you know, and be successful in the things that you didn't know. Stevens: You work in a very creative industry, how do you keep your staff motivated in this industry, how do you keep them going, how do you keep them working for you? Tam: I always tell them my story, how I was in school when my teacher asked for one outfit -- I give them 8 outfits. I told them, do things that I didn't ask you, give me, do your work with passion, it's more important than "Oh, 6 o'clock, I have to leave." Do something that is out of the box. E-mail to a friend .

HONG KONG, China (CNN) -- From the runway to the store rack, Vivienne Tam is a designer who blends creativity with business acumen in equal measure. The acclaimed fashion designer spoke with CNN's Andrew Stevens in The Boardroom. Since launching her career in the fashion industry in the early 1980s and founding her own brand in the 1990s, Tam has risen to prominence through her signature east-meets-west aesthetic. Today, it is her business acumen that has expanded her label to roughly 30 stores worldwide, spanning cities from New York to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens met with the designer in Hong Kong to discuss what it takes to steer both the business and creative direction of a global fashion brand.

Tam: The business side is much like designing—I appreciate the feel of the fabric, I want to know every detail. You develop an instinct for it, an understanding of what makes a good deal, because who better to know what's best for you than yourself? It's the same as designing clothes: I love figuring out how to solve every challenge, whether it's determining the right budget or anything else.

Stevens: So it's simply natural curiosity?

Tam: Natural curiosity, yes—I love it. I love every aspect of it.

Stevens: Who taught you your business skills, or did you learn as you went along?

Tam: I'm entirely self-taught in business. I knew nothing when I started—I learned everything about pricing, shipping, contracts, all of it, simply by doing it. When you handle things yourself, you truly understand them. If you don't, and you simply listen to someone else explain how it's done, you never gain that firsthand experience. But once you experience it yourself, you grow tremendously from it—you can go so much further. It becomes intuitive.

Stevens: When you were named Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year, you said your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you?

Tam: She inspired me profoundly—through her determination and persistence, as you mentioned. When she set her mind to accomplishing something, she would see it through to the very end; she was truly determined to make it happen. I saw her as the driving force behind me. We were quite poor growing up—my parents worked incredibly hard with very little money. Watching them work so tirelessly instilled in me a deep desire to change our circumstances, to build something meaningful.

Stevens: What do you consider the most important qualities for a businessperson to possess?

Tam: For me, the essentials are vision, determination, and never allowing yourself to say no. You must remain open to criticism and open to learning. Starting out knowing nothing about business can actually work in your favor—it allows you to learn everything from scratch and find success in areas where you initially had no expertise.

Stevens: You work in a highly creative industry—how do you keep your staff motivated and engaged, and how do you inspire their continued commitment to your vision?

Tam: I always share my own story with them—how, back in school, when a teacher asked for one outfit, I would deliver eight. I tell my team: don't just do what's asked of you—go beyond it. Approach your work with passion; that matters far more than simply clocking out at six o'clock. Do something that pushes beyond the ordinary, something that breaks the mold.

# Vivienne Tam: Balancing Design and Business Success

**HONG KONG, China (CNN)** — Vivienne Tam exemplifies the rare designer who blends artistic vision with sharp commercial instincts. CNN correspondent Andrew Stevens sat down with the renowned fashion figure during a segment for The Boardroom.

Tam entered the fashion industry in the early 1980s and later launched her own label in the following decade, gaining recognition for her signature fusion of Eastern and Western aesthetics. Her business savvy has since propelled the brand's growth to approximately 30 locations across the globe, spanning cities from New York to Beijing. Stevens met with her in Hong Kong to discuss the challenges of simultaneously overseeing both the artistic and commercial sides of an international fashion empire.

**Tam:** Running the business feels a lot like designing to me—I appreciate understanding the fine details, much like I appreciate the texture of fabric. You develop an instinct for negotiations because, really, who else would look out for your best interests better than you yourself? It mirrors the design process, where I enjoy tackling every challenge that arises, whether it's figuring out budgets or something else entirely.

**Stevens:** So it stems from natural curiosity?

**Tam:** Exactly, pure curiosity drives me. I find joy in every element of it.

**Stevens:** Where did you develop your business acumen—did you have mentors, or did you figure it out through trial and error?

**Tam:** I'm entirely self-taught when it comes to business. I started with zero knowledge and learned everything hands-on—pricing strategies, logistics, contract negotiations, all of it. Hands-on experience teaches you things that simply listening to advice never can. Real understanding comes from doing the work yourself, and that's what allows you to progress and eventually excel far beyond where you started. It's something you have to feel through experience.

**Stevens:** After receiving the Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year award, you credited your mother as a major source of inspiration. Can you elaborate on that?

**Tam:** She shaped me profoundly—her tenacity and unwavering commitment left a lasting impression. Whenever she set her mind to accomplishing something, she pursued it relentlessly until it was done. She remains a driving force in my life. Growing up, my family struggled financially, and I watched my parents labor tirelessly just to get by. Witnessing their sacrifices ignited something in me—a deep desire to transform our circumstances and build something meaningful of my own.

**Stevens:** What qualities do you consider essential for succeeding in business?

**Tam:** For me, having a clear vision matters most, along with persistence and refusing to limit yourself. Staying receptive to feedback and remaining a perpetual student are equally crucial. Interestingly, starting out with no business background at all meant I had to absorb everything from scratch—and that ignorance became a foundation for genuine achievement in areas I initially knew nothing about.

**Stevens:** Given that you operate in such a creative field, how do you maintain motivation among your team members and keep them committed to your vision?

**Tam:** I frequently share a story from my school days—when a teacher requested just one outfit, I delivered eight instead. I encourage my team to exceed expectations without being asked, to approach their work with genuine enthusiasm rather than clock-watching until the workday ends. I push them to think creatively and step beyond conventional boundaries.

# Vivienne Tam: Where Creativity Meets Commerce

Vivienne Tam stands as one of the fashion industry's most accomplished figures, distinguished by her rare ability to seamlessly blend artistic vision with shrewd business sense. As the driving force behind her own global fashion label, she has demonstrated that creative talent and commercial success are not mutually exclusive—rather, they can be powerful complements to one another when approached with equal dedication.

## A Journey Built on Experience

Tam's path to success has been marked by steady, deliberate growth. She first entered the fashion business in the early 1980s, gaining foundational experience in an industry she would eventually come to lead. It wasn't until the 1990s that she took the pivotal step of establishing her own brand, transforming her accumulated knowledge and creative instincts into a namesake label. From that starting point, her business has expanded remarkably, growing to encompass approximately 30 stores across the globe. Her retail footprint now spans an impressive geographic range, from the fashion capital of New York to the bustling markets of Beijing, reflecting both the universal appeal of her designs and her strategic vision for global expansion.

## The Business of Passion

What sets Tam apart is her holistic approach to running a fashion enterprise. Rather than viewing design and business as separate spheres, she brings the same intensity of passion and curiosity to both. This integrated mindset means she finds genuine satisfaction not only in the creative process of designing collections but also in the granular details of running a company—understanding fabric compositions with the same enthusiasm she applies to negotiating deals or managing budgets. For Tam, fulfillment comes from mastering the complete picture of her business, leaving no aspect unexamined or delegated without understanding.

## Self-Taught Business Acumen

Perhaps most striking is that Tam's business expertise was not acquired through formal training or mentorship in traditional corporate settings. Instead, she is entirely self-taught, having developed her understanding of critical business functions—pricing strategies, shipping logistics, and contract negotiations—through direct, hands-on experience. Rather than being instructed on proper procedures, she learned by doing, encountering challenges and solving them in real time. This experiential approach to business education has given her a practical, grounded understanding of her industry that theoretical knowledge alone could not provide.

## A Mother's Influence

Behind Tam's professional achievements lies a deeply personal source of inspiration: her mother. Tam has openly credited her mother's determination and persistence as foundational qualities that have shaped her own philosophy toward both work and life more broadly. This maternal influence appears to have instilled in Tam the resilience necessary to navigate the challenges of building a business from the ground up, as well as the tenacity required to sustain and grow that business across decades and continents. Her mother's example serves as a reminder that the qualities driving professional success often have their roots in personal relationships and early life lessons.

Through this combination of creative talent, self-taught business savvy, and inherited determination, Vivienne Tam has built not just a fashion label, but a lasting testament to the power of merging passion with pragmatism.

# From Sketchbook to Storefront: Vivienne Tam's Self-Made Success

When Vivienne Tam launched her fashion label in the 1980s, she had a clear creative vision but little formal training in the business mechanics that would ultimately determine whether that vision could survive in a competitive global marketplace. Decades later, her brand—known for its distinctive fusion of Eastern and Western aesthetics—has grown into an international label with approximately 30 stores across the world. In a recent interview, Tam opened up about the unconventional path she took to get there, revealing that much of what she knows about running a fashion business came not from mentors or business school, but from rolling up her sleeves and figuring things out herself.

Rather than delegating the less glamorous aspects of the industry to others, Tam made a deliberate choice early on to immerse herself in the granular details of the business. She personally negotiated pricing structures, managed the complexities of shipping and logistics, and pored over contracts—tasks that many designers might consider outside their creative purview or better left to specialized staff. This hands-on involvement meant confronting a steep learning curve, but Tam saw it as essential to understanding her business from the ground up rather than operating at a remove from its practical realities.

"I had to learn by doing," she explained, describing how she approached unfamiliar aspects of the industry not with intimidation but with curiosity. This willingness to dive into unknown territory, she says, became one of the defining traits that shaped her entrepreneurial journey. Instead of waiting for someone else to explain how the industry worked, she sought out answers herself, treating each new challenge—whether it was a complicated shipping contract or a pricing negotiation—as an opportunity to expand her own expertise.

Tam is quick to point out that this drive didn't emerge in a vacuum. She credits her mother's example of determination and persistence as a formative influence, one that shaped her own resilience when faced with the inevitable setbacks and complications of building a business from scratch. Watching her mother navigate difficulties with steady resolve gave Tam a model for how to approach her own obstacles: not with avoidance, but with a willingness to push through discomfort in pursuit of long-term goals.

Taken together, Tam's story illustrates a broader truth about entrepreneurship in creative industries: success often depends as much on grit and self-education as it does on innate talent or artistic vision. Her career demonstrates how personal curiosity, combined with lessons absorbed from family and life experience, can become powerful engines for both creative expression and sustainable business growth. For Tam, the fashion label she built wasn't just a showcase for her design sensibilities—it became a testament to what's possible when someone is willing to learn the unglamorous fundamentals of an industry firsthand, rather than relying solely on the guidance or expertise of others.

# Hong Kong: A Bridge Between East and West

Hong Kong stands as one of the world's most dynamic global financial centers, a testament to the unique confluence of cultures, economic systems, and histories that have shaped it. Since its handover from British colonial rule to China in 1997, Hong Kong has operated under the "One Country, Two Systems" framework, allowing it to maintain its own economic and administrative systems distinct from mainland China while remaining part of the People's Republic of China.

This special administrative region has long served as a crucial gateway connecting China to global markets. Its strategic location, deep-water harbor, and business-friendly environment helped transform it from a modest trading post into a bustling metropolis renowned for its skyline, financial markets, and vibrant culture. The territory's legal system, based on English common law, coexists alongside its integration with mainland China's broader governance structure.

Hong Kong's relationship with China has evolved significantly over the decades. The city has been instrumental in facilitating foreign investment into China and serving as a testing ground for economic reforms. Its stock exchange remains one of Asia's largest, attracting both Chinese and international companies seeking capital.

Culturally, Hong Kong represents a fascinating blend of Cantonese traditions, British colonial influences, and modern Chinese identity. Cuisine, language, festivals, and daily life all reflect this multifaceted heritage. Cantonese remains the predominant spoken language, though Mandarin and English are also widely used, particularly in business and government contexts.

In recent years, Hong Kong has navigated complex questions about its identity, autonomy, and future within the broader Chinese nation. These discussions touch on governance, civil liberties, and the balance between local autonomy and national integration—topics that continue to shape conversations both within the territory and internationally.

Despite these complexities, Hong Kong remains an essential node in global commerce, a cultural crossroads, and a unique expression of how different systems and traditions can coexist within a single, evolving political framework.

# THE BOARDROOM
### CNN International
**Featuring: Vivienne Tam, Fashion Designer**

---

**ANDREW STEVENS:** Welcome to The Boardroom. My guest today has built a fashion empire that bridges East and West — literally and stylistically. Vivienne Tam, welcome to the program.

**VIVIENNE TAM:** Thank you, Andrew. It's a pleasure to be here.

**STEVENS:** You've often described yourself as a bridge between Chinese heritage and Western fashion sensibilities. Where did that begin?

**TAM:** I was born in Guangzhou, raised in Hong Kong — so from the very beginning, I had this duality. Hong Kong itself is East meeting West. Then I moved to New York in the 1980s to study fashion, and suddenly I was seeing my own culture through completely new eyes. I realized nobody was really translating Chinese aesthetics for a global, contemporary audience. That became my mission, in a way.

**STEVENS:** Your "Mao Collection" in the 1990s put you on the international map. That was a bold move — taking one of the most politically loaded images in modern Chinese history and turning it into fashion.

**TAM:** It was risky, yes. But I wanted to reclaim the image — to say, this is part of our visual history, and we can look at it with irony, with humor, even with affection, rather than only through a political lens. Andy Warhol had done his Mao series, and I wanted a Chinese designer's perspective on that iconography. It resonated because people were curious about China, but China was still somewhat closed off to the world's imagination. I gave people a way in.

**STEVENS:** Let's talk business. You've built Vivienne Tam into a global brand — collections, fragrances, partnerships with companies like HP for a limited-edition laptop. How do you think about brand extension versus staying purely a fashion house?

**TAM:** For me, design isn't just clothing — it's a philosophy, an aesthetic point of view. So when the right partnership comes along, something that lets me tell a story visually, I'm open to it. The HP laptop was fun because it took fashion into technology, into people's everyday work lives. It wasn't about diluting the brand; it was about extending the reach of the ideas.

**STEVENS:** China's own domestic fashion industry has grown enormously since you started your career. Do you see Chinese designers today as competitors, or as part of the same movement you helped start?

**TAM:** Part of the same movement, absolutely. When I began, there was almost no infrastructure — no supply chain sophistication, limited global visibility for Chinese talent. Now you have incredible young designers coming out of Shanghai, Beijing, showing in Paris and Milan. I feel proud, honestly. I always say I want to open doors, not guard them.

**STEVENS:** How has doing business in China changed for you over the decades?

**TAM:** Dramatically. Manufacturing capabilities are far more advanced. The Chinese consumer is more sophisticated, more brand-aware, and increasingly proud of homegrown design rather than only looking to Western luxury labels. That's a real shift — a kind of cultural confidence that wasn't there when I started.

**STEVENS:** Is there tension in being seen as "the Chinese designer" in New York, versus just "a designer" who happens to be Chinese?

**TAM:** There's always a question of labels. But I've made peace with it — my heritage is my strength, not a limitation. I don't want to be boxed in only as "ethnic" or "exotic," but I also don't want to erase where I come from to fit into someone else's idea of universal. My hope is that the work speaks for itself, culturally specific and globally relevant at the same time.

**STEVENS:** Finally — advice for young designers, particularly from Asia, trying to break into an industry still centered in Paris, Milan, New York?

**TAM:** Know your story. The industry has enough people copying trends. What's valuable is a genuine point of view — something only you can say, based on where you come from and how you see the world. That's what travels. That's what lasts.

**STEVENS:** Vivienne Tam, thank you for joining us on The Boardroom.

**TAM:** Thank you, Andrew.

---

*[END SEGMENT]*

# From Sketchbook to Empire: How Fashion Visionary Mei Lin Chen Built a Global Brand

*CNN Style*

When Mei Lin Chen launched her eponymous fashion label from a cramped Shanghai apartment 15 years ago, few could have predicted it would become one of Asia's most influential design houses, with flagship stores in six countries and a client list that includes A-list celebrities and royalty.

Chen, 42, has carved out a distinctive niche by blending traditional Chinese textile techniques with contemporary silhouettes, creating pieces that feel both timeless and utterly modern. Her label, MEI, reported revenues exceeding $80 million last year, and she was recently named to a prominent list of Asia's most influential business leaders.

CNN sat down with Chen at her Shanghai headquarters to discuss creativity, resilience, and what it really takes to build a lasting brand.

**CNN: You started this company with almost no capital. What kept you going in those early years?**

**Chen:** Honestly? Stubbornness. [Laughs] I had bankers and even my own family tell me the market didn't need another fashion brand. But I wasn't trying to create "another" brand — I was trying to solve a specific problem. I wanted to show that Chinese craftsmanship could exist in the luxury space without being reduced to costume or cliché. That vision was clear enough that I could survive the rejections.

**CNN: How would you describe your design philosophy?**

**Chen:** Restraint. I think there's a misconception that heritage-inspired design means maximalism — lots of embroidery, lots of color. For me, it's the opposite. I want to take one traditional element, maybe a weaving technique from Suzhou, and let it breathe in a modern silhouette. The craftsmanship should feel discovered, not shouted.

**CNN: You've talked before about failure being essential to your process. Can you elaborate?**

**Chen:** Every collection has pieces that die in the studio. I mean that literally — samples get cut apart, fabric gets thrown away. Early in my career, I was devastated by this. Now I see it as the cost of doing anything interesting. If everything you make succeeds immediately, you're probably not pushing hard enough.

**CNN: As a woman running a company in an industry still dominated by male executives at the top levels, what obstacles have you faced?**

**Chen:** There were moments early on where investors would speak to my male business partner instead of me, even though it was my name on the label and my vision driving everything. I learned to stop being polite about correcting that. Competence should not require constant re-proving, but sometimes it does, and you have to be ready for that fight without letting it exhaust you.

**CNN: What advice do you give to young designers trying to break into the industry today?**

**Chen:** Stop trying to please everyone. I see so many young designers create collections that are technically accomplished but say nothing. Have a point of view, even if it alienates some people. The designers I respect most are the ones I can identify blindfolded, just from the feel of the construction or the proportions. That specificity is worth more than broad appeal.

**CNN: Looking ahead, what's next for the brand?**

**Chen:** We're expanding into home goods, which excites me because it's a totally different design problem. But the throughline will remain the same: quiet luxury, authentic craftsmanship, nothing shouted. I want people to live inside our aesthetic, not just wear it.

*Mei Lin Chen's latest collection debuts in Paris next month.*

# Hong Kong Fashion Entrepreneur Weaves Family Legacy Into Sustainable Business Empire

**HONG KONG** — In a bustling showroom overlooking Victoria Harbour, sample garments in jewel tones hang alongside mood boards tracing three generations of design influence. Here, entrepreneur Mei-Lin Chao is building what she calls "a bridge between old craft and new conscience" — a fashion label that has grown from a single market stall to a multi-million dollar business with a growing international footprint.

Chao, 41, founded her label, Lin & Heritage, eight years ago after leaving a corporate finance career. Today the company employs more than 200 people across Hong Kong and manufacturing partners in Vietnam and Cambodia, with a growing emphasis on sustainable textiles and fair labor practices.

"I didn't set out to build a company," Chao told CNN in an interview at her Kowloon office. "I set out to solve a problem — that the industry I loved was hurting the people and places that made it possible. The business grew because the mission was bigger than me."

## A Family Thread

Chao credits her grandmother, a seamstress who fled to Hong Kong in the 1950s, as her earliest inspiration.

"She had nothing when she arrived, but she had her hands and her needle," Chao said. "I still have her sewing box. When I doubt myself, I open it — not because it has answers, but because it reminds me what resilience actually looks like."

Her mother, too, shaped her approach to business, Chao said, particularly around the idea that success should be communal rather than singular.

"My mother used to say, 'A rising tide should lift more than your own boat.' That stuck with me. It's why we've built profit-sharing into our factory partnerships, not just charity add-ons," she said.

## Leadership Philosophy

Chao's leadership style, she says, has been deliberately shaped against the hierarchical corporate culture she left behind.

"I don't believe in leadership as command," she said. "I believe in leadership as translation — translating a vision so clearly that people don't need to be told what to do; they already know, because they helped build it."

She pointed to her management team, many of whom she promoted from factory-floor roles, as evidence of that philosophy in action.

"The best ideas in this company rarely come from the top floor," Chao said. "They come from the person who's been stitching sleeves for fifteen years and knows exactly where the fabric wastes ten seconds of time — multiplied by a thousand garments."

## Motivation Beyond Profit

Asked what keeps her motivated after nearly a decade of 80-hour weeks, Chao paused before answering.

"Money was never the motivator — it's the fuel, not the destination," she said. "What motivates me is walking through our factories and seeing workers who send their kids to school on wages that didn't exist in this industry five years ago. That's the metric that matters to me."

She acknowledged the personal cost of entrepreneurship, including strained relationships and health scares from overwork early in the company's history.

"There were years I sacrificed too much," she admitted. "But I've learned that sustainability isn't just about fabric and supply chains — it has to apply to the people running the company too. I burned out once. I don't intend to again."

## Looking Ahead

Lin & Heritage plans to open its first retail flagship outside Asia next year, with a store slated for London. Chao says she also hopes to formalize an apprenticeship program modeled on the informal mentorship she received from her grandmother.

"She taught me that beautiful things take patience," Chao said, gesturing to a rack of hand-finished silk blouses nearby. "In an industry obsessed with speed, I want to prove that patience is still a competitive advantage — and that where you come from can be the very thing that carries you forward."

*This story is a work of fiction created for illustrative purposes.*

# Behind the Seams: A Conversation on Creativity and Commerce

*CNN Style Correspondent sits down with independent fashion designer Elena Marchetti, founder of the eponymous label that's grown from a one-woman operation to a 15-person studio in six years.*

---

**CNN:** Elena, thank you for making time for this. Let's start with something a lot of creative entrepreneurs struggle with—how do you balance the artistic side of design with the business decisions that keep the lights on?

**Elena Marchetti:** Honestly, it took me years to stop treating them as enemies. Early on, I thought business thinking would poison my creativity—like if I started worrying about margins, I'd lose whatever made my work interesting. But I've realized the opposite is true. Understanding your numbers actually *protects* your creative freedom. If I know exactly what a collection costs to produce, I can fight harder for the design choices that matter to me instead of getting steamrolled by budget conversations I don't understand.

**CNN:** So the business literacy came later?

**Elena Marchetti:** Much later, and mostly out of necessity. I didn't go to business school. I taught myself accounting basics from YouTube videos and a lot of very patient conversations with my accountant, where I probably asked embarrassingly simple questions. I learned pattern-making from library books before I could afford proper training. There's this myth that self-taught means less rigorous, but honestly, it made me obsessive. When you have to figure something out yourself, you don't just learn the rule—you learn *why* the rule exists.

**CNN:** Was there a moment you remember feeling like you'd crossed over from "designer" to "business owner"?

**Elena Marchetti:** The day I had to let someone go because we couldn't afford the position anymore. That wrecked me. Design school doesn't prepare you for that. That's when the business side stopped being abstract spreadsheet stuff and became about real people's lives.

**CNN:** Speaking of people—you now manage a team of fifteen. How do you keep everyone motivated, especially in an industry known for burnout?

**Elena Marchetti:** I try to remember that everyone on my team could probably work somewhere with better pay or more stability. They stay because they believe in what we're building. So my job is to make sure that belief is rewarded—not just with paychecks, though obviously that matters, but with real ownership over their work. My head patternmaker isn't just executing my sketches; she's problem-solving, pushing back when something won't work, making it better. I have to actually listen, not just perform listening.

**CNN:** Any specific practices that help with that?

**Elena Marchetti:** Transparency, mostly. I tell my team when a collection isn't selling well. I tell them when we've had a great wholesale order come in. People can smell fake positivity, and they can also handle bad news better than being kept in the dark. I'd rather have hard conversations early than watch morale erode from uncertainty.

**CNN:** Last question—what would you tell a young designer who's terrified of the business side?

**Elena Marchetti:** Stop treating it like a betrayal of your art. Nobody hands you permission to keep making beautiful things—you have to build the container that lets that happen. Learn to read a balance sheet. It's just another material, like fabric. You wouldn't refuse to learn how silk drapes differently than wool. Same thing.

**CNN:** Elena Marchetti, thank you so much for your candor.

**Elena Marchetti:** Thank you for having me.

# CNN BOARDROOM
## Segment: "The Founder's Journey"

**[STUDIO - CNN BOARDROOM SET]**

**ANCHOR (RICHARD CHEN):** Welcome back to Boardroom. Today we're joined by a woman who transformed a small atelier into a global fashion house spanning forty countries. Please welcome the founder and creative director of Lumière Noir, Amara Okafor-Williams. Amara, thank you for joining us.

**AMARA OKAFOR-WILLIAMS:** Thank you for having me, Richard. It's always a pleasure to be back in New York.

**CHEN:** Let's start at the beginning. You didn't come from money, you didn't go to a prestigious fashion school. Walk us through those early days.

**AMARA:** People often assume there's this glamorous origin story, but honestly, mine started in my mother's kitchen in Lagos. She was a seamstress—not a designer, a seamstress. She made school uniforms, wedding dresses, whatever paid the bills that week. I used to sit under her sewing table doing homework while she worked twelve-hour days.

**CHEN:** How did that shape your relationship with the industry?

**AMARA:** It gave me respect for craft before I ever understood branding or marketing. My mother used to say, "Amara, a stitch that's rushed is a stitch that shows." She wasn't talking about fashion philosophy—she was talking about paying rent. But that phrase has guided every collection I've ever released.

**CHEN:** You immigrated to London at nineteen. That transition must have been jarring.

**AMARA:** [laughs] Jarring is generous. I arrived with two suitcases and about £300. I worked in a fabric warehouse during the day and took night classes in pattern-making. I wasn't networking at galas—I was learning to survive winter for the first time in my life.

**CHEN:** When did the idea for Lumière Noir actually take shape?

**AMARA:** Around year six. I'd saved enough to make ten dresses—just ten—using West African textile techniques my mother taught me, but with silhouettes influenced by what I was seeing in London and Paris. I sold them at a market stall in Brixton. A stylist happened to walk by, bought one for a client, and that client wore it to an award show. That's the story everyone wants—the lucky break. But it took six years of unglamorous groundwork before that "lucky" moment could even happen.

**CHEN:** There's a lesson in that alone. Let's talk about scaling. Going from ten dresses to a global brand is an entirely different skill set.

**AMARA:** Completely different. Design got me in the door, but business acumen kept the doors open. I had to learn supply chains, retail margins, negotiating with distributors who didn't take me seriously because I was young, Black, and a woman in rooms that weren't built for any of those identities.

**CHEN:** How did you push through that?

**AMARA:** I stopped asking for permission. I started asking for partnership. There's a difference in energy. When you walk in asking "will you let me," people sense desperation. When you walk in saying "here's what we'll build together," the dynamic shifts.

**CHEN:** Your mother passed away six years ago, correct? How present is her influence in the company today?

**AMARA:** Every single collection carries her name somewhere—sometimes literally stitched into the lining, sometimes in the technique, sometimes just in spirit. We have a program now, funded by the company, that trains young seamstresses in Lagos and pays them fair wages while they learn design fundamentals. It's called the Adaeze Fund, after her.

**CHEN:** That's beautiful. Let's talk to our viewers who are early in their entrepreneurial journey. What's the advice you find yourself repeating most often?

**AMARA:** Three things. First—master your craft before you master your marketing. Too many people build a beautiful brand around a mediocre product, and eventually that catches up with you.

Second—your first version doesn't need to be perfect, it needs to exist. I sold ten imperfect dresses in a market stall. I didn't wait until I had a flagship store and a runway show.

Third, and this is the one people resist most: build slowly enough that you don't lose yourself. I've seen brilliant founders burn out or compromise their values chasing speed. Sustainable growth isn't just an environmental term—it applies to your business and your soul.

**CHEN:** Final question. If you could go back and speak to yourself in that fabric warehouse in London, what would you say?

**AMARA:** [pauses] I'd say—the exhaustion is temporary, but the discipline you're building is permanent. Don't rush toward the applause. Rush toward the mastery. The applause finds you eventually.

**CHEN:** Amara Okafor-Williams, founder of Lumière Noir. Thank you for sharing your story with us.

**AMARA:** Thank you, Richard.

**CHEN:** When we return—the economics of sustainable manufacturing, and why more brands are following Amara's lead. Stay with us.

**[BREAK]**

---

*[END OF SEGMENT]*
